***
# Summary

An MR1 data package holds the data of one radar campaign (e.g. `CH_Sempach_2024`)
in a standardised, self-describing format: the
[Frictionless Data Package](https://datapackage.org). It consists of one CSV
file per table and a `datapackage.json` file that describes the tables (column
types, descriptions, units, and how the tables link to each other) and the
campaign (title, contributors, licence, embargo, location, period, ...).

Each campaign package is published as its own dataset on Zenodo, with its own
DOI. These campaign datasets are grouped in owner collections (e.g. all
campaigns of the Swiss Ornithological Institute) and in a community collection
(all BirdScan MR1 campaigns), so users can cite the level that matches their
study.

The workflow has 5 steps:

1.    Extract the data from the SQL database.

2.    (optional) Load the manual blind times.

3.    Describe the campaign in a metadata file.

4.    Create the data package.

5.    Upload the data package to Zenodo.

***
# Before we get started

We first load the birdscanR package and set an output directory.
```{r}
library(birdscanR)

# Set main output directory
# =============================================================================
mainOutputDir = tempdir()
```

***
# Step 1: Extract the data from the SQL database

The data package is created from the output of `extractDbData()`. For a real
campaign, you extract the data from your database as described in the
vignette "Introduction to birdscanR". Extract all data of the campaign, with
all the echo features you want to publish:
```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Extract the data from the SQL database
# =============================================================================
dbData = extractDbData(
  dbDriverChar              = "SQL Server",
  dbServer                  = "MACHINE\\SERVERNAME",
  dbName                    = "CH_Sempach_2024",
  saveDbToFile              = TRUE,
  dbDataDir                 = mainOutputDir,
  radarTimeZone             = "Etc/GMT0",
  targetTimeZone            = "Etc/GMT0",
  listOfRfFeaturesToExtract = c(167, 168),
  siteLocation              = c(47.12764, 8.192569),
  sunOrCivil                = "civil",
  crepuscule                = "nauticalSolar"
)
```

In this vignette, we use the sample data extract that ships with the package:
two days (24-25 September 2024) of data from the radar at Sempach,
Switzerland.
```{r}
# Load example data
# =============================================================================
dbData = readRDS(system.file("extdata",
  "CH_Sempach_2024_SEP24_25_DataExtract.rds",
  package = "birdscanR"
))
dbName = "CH_Sempach_2024_SEP24_25"
```

***
# Step 2: (optional) Load the manual blind times

Manual blind times are periods in which the radar data should not be used,
e.g. because of rain or technical problems, that were noted by the radar
operator. They are stored in a csv file and loaded with
`loadManualBlindTimes()`. `createDataPackage()` merges them with the blind
times registered by the radar, so that the package holds one blind time table.

The csv file has one row per blind time and three columns without header:
start and stop time (`yyyy-mm-dd hh:mm:ss`) and the type of blind time. The
package contains an example (`data(manualBlindTimes)`) with three blind times
during the sample data: rain on the morning of 24 September, a technical
outage in the night of 24-25 September, and clutter on the afternoon of 25
September. We write it to a csv file, as you would have it for a real
campaign, and load it:
```{r}
# Write the example manual blind times to a csv file (normally you already
# have this file)
# =============================================================================
data(manualBlindTimes)
manualBlindTimes
manualBlindTimesFile = file.path(mainOutputDir, "manualBlindTimes_Sempach.csv")
write.table(manualBlindTimes,
  file = manualBlindTimesFile, sep = ",",
  row.names = FALSE, col.names = FALSE
)

# Load the manual blind times
# =============================================================================
cManualBlindTimes = loadManualBlindTimes(
  filePath     = manualBlindTimesFile,
  blindTimesTZ = "Etc/GMT0",
  targetTZ     = "Etc/GMT0"
)
```
If there are no manual blind times, set `cManualBlindTimes = NULL`.

***
# Step 3: Describe the campaign in a metadata file

The description of the campaign is stored in a YAML file, one per campaign.
Write a template with `createDataPackageMetadataTemplate()` and fill it in with
a text editor:
```{r}
# Write the metadata template
# =============================================================================
metadataFile = file.path(mainOutputDir, "CH_Sempach_2024_metadata.yaml")
createDataPackageMetadataTemplate(filePath = metadataFile, overwrite = TRUE)
```

The template contains the following fields (shown here with the example
values of the template):
```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(metadataFile), sep = "\n")
```

A few points to consider when you fill it in:

- **campaignID**: `<country code>_<site>_<year>`, e.g. `CH_Sempach_2024`. It is
  used as the name of the package and of the output folder.
- **licenses**: `CC-BY-4.0` or `CC-BY-NC-4.0`.
- **embargo**: the date until which the data files stay restricted on Zenodo.
  The metadata (and thus the existence of the dataset, its contributors and
  how to contact them) are always public. If you leave it empty, the embargo
  ends 5 years after the last data in the package.
- **contributors**: list everyone who should get credit for the dataset. Each
  contributor needs one or more roles out of `ContactPerson`, `ProjectLeader`,
  `DataCollector`, `DataCurator`, `Researcher`, `RightsHolder` and
  `Supervisor`. At least one contributor must be the `ContactPerson`. Give the
  ORCID of each contributor whenever possible: it is used to merge the
  contributors of all campaigns into the creators of the collections.
- **embargoRequestType**: how a contributor wants to be involved when someone
  requests the data during the embargo: `1` = contact me (potential
  collaborator), `2` = citation only.

You can also build or adjust the metadata in R, and pass a list instead of a
file. Here, for example, we add a second contributor:
```{r}
# Adjust the metadata in R
# =============================================================================
metadata = yaml::read_yaml(metadataFile)
metadata$contributors[[2]] = list(
  title              = "Baptiste Schmid",
  givenName          = "Baptiste",
  familyName         = "Schmid",
  path               = "https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7736-7527",
  organization       = "Swiss Ornithological Institute",
  roles              = c("ProjectLeader", "DataCollector"),
  embargoRequestType = 1
)
```

The metadata are checked when the data package is created. If something is
missing or wrong, `createDataPackage()` stops and lists all problems, e.g.:
```{r, error = TRUE}
badMetadata = metadata
badMetadata$title = NULL
badMetadata$contributors[[2]]$roles = "Author"
createDataPackage(dbExtract = dbData, metadata = badMetadata)
```

***
# Step 4: Create the data package

`createDataPackage()` selects the data of the campaign, applies the filters you
set, and builds the data package. The filters are the same as in
`filterProtocolData()` and `filterEchoData()`; they are stored in the package
metadata, so users know how the data were selected. For a data package, you
normally keep all data of the campaign and only exclude what should not be
published (e.g. a test period at the start of the campaign).
```{r}
# Create the MR1 data package
# =============================================================================
dataPackage = createDataPackage(
  dbExtract         = dbData,
  metadata          = metadata,
  manualBlindTimes  = cManualBlindTimes,
  dbName            = dbName,
  timeRangeTargetTZ = c("2024-09-24 00:00", "2024-09-25 23:59"),
  outputDirPath     = mainOutputDir
)
dataPackage
```

## What is in the data package?

The package holds five tables (resources):

| Resource         | Content                                                                 |
|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `echo_data`      | Echoes, with their features, classification and MTR factors             |
| `protocol_data`  | Measurement periods (protocols) with their radar settings               |
| `blind_times`    | Periods in which the radar could not detect echoes                      |
| `sunrise_sunset` | Sunrise, sunset and twilight times at the site                          |
| `site_data`      | Location of the radar and radar/calibration parameters                  |

Read a table as a data frame with `frictionless::read_resource()`:
```{r}
# Read the blind times
# =============================================================================
blindTimes = frictionless::read_resource(dataPackage, "blind_times")
head(blindTimes)
table(blindTimes$type)
```

Each table has a schema that describes its columns, and how it links to the
other tables: each echo belongs to a measurement period (`protocolID`), and
each measurement period to a site (`siteID`).
```{r}
# Show the schema of the protocol table
# =============================================================================
protocolSchema = frictionless::get_schema(dataPackage, "protocol_data")
data.frame(
  name        = sapply(protocolSchema$fields, function(x) x$name),
  type        = sapply(protocolSchema$fields, function(x) x$type),
  description = sapply(protocolSchema$fields, function(x) x$description)
)
str(protocolSchema[c("primaryKey", "foreignKeys")])
```

Besides the metadata from the YAML file, `createDataPackage()` adds the
location and period of the campaign, the applied filters, the provenance of
the data (database, birdscanR and classifier versions), and a suggested
citation:
```{r}
# Show some of the package metadata
# =============================================================================
dataPackage$embargo
dataPackage$temporal
dataPackage$spatial
dataPackage$bibliographicCitation
str(dataPackage$`mr1dp:provenance`)
```

## The files on disk

Because we set `outputDirPath`, the package was written to a folder named after
the `campaignID`. This folder is what you upload to Zenodo:
```{r}
packageDir = file.path(mainOutputDir, "CH_Sempach_2024")
list.files(packageDir)
```

Anyone can read the package back, with R or any other software that supports
Frictionless Data Packages:
```{r}
# Read the data package from disk
# =============================================================================
dataPackageFromDisk = frictionless::read_package(file.path(packageDir, "datapackage.json"))
echoData = frictionless::read_resource(dataPackageFromDisk, "echo_data")
dim(echoData)
```
